transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2026-09-02
Time: 16:00 UTC
Duration: 52 minutes
Attendees: Ari Kaplan (Redwood AE), Jordan Meyers (Redwood SE), Lina Morales (Product Lead, Auriga), Raj Patel (Platform Eng, Auriga), Maya Chen (Security, Auriga), Ethan Ross (ML Eng, Auriga)

Auto-summary (auto-generated, may be imperfect):
Redwood walked Auriga through structured output (JSON mode) + tool/function calling, focusing on typed responses, schema enforcement, and multi-tier fallback routing. Discussed tradeoffs for hosted vs private (VPC) deployments, KMS and log audit controls, and a pilot scope for runtime guardrails and schema-first integration. Action items and next steps agreed.

--- Transcript body ---
[00:00] Ari (AE): Hey everyone, thanks for joining. Quick roll call — can you hear me?
[00:03] Lina (Auriga): Yep sounds good, Ari.
[00:05] Raj (Auriga): Loud and clear.
[00:07] Jordan (SE): Hi all, Jordan here — I'll drive the demo portion with the runtime bits.
[00:11] Maya (Auriga): Maya joins, hi.

[00:28] Ari: Okay great, agenda for today: high level overview of JSON-mode typed outputs, then Jordan will show a workflow in Console + API, we'll talk about fallbacks and routing patterns from Redwood Optimize, then Q&A and pilot next steps.

[01:03] Lina: We're most interested in guarantees around structure — our product relies on deterministic JSON responses for downstream eventing. We also have strict PII rules and want to know how guardrails prevent hallucinated fields.

[01:20] Jordan: Totally, and we hear that a lot. We'll demo schema enforcement, plus typed responses with schema validation hooks. Note that the SDKs let you declare a schema and Redwood will try to adhere and if it fails the runtime can either reject, auto-correct with best-effort, or invoke a tool to repair the payload.

[01:46] Ethan (Auriga): When you say "invoke a tool" — is that function calling like OpenAI's tooling or is it Redwood's own runtime?

[01:55] Jordan: It's our runtime orchestration. You can register external services as tools — e.g., a normalization microservice or a DB write op — and Redwood will call them using the structured output contract. We attach typed signatures to the call so the tool receives predictable args. Small caveat: sometimes the transcriber says, the tool calling's names might get garbled in the transcript, like "to call the K-V cash" — that's K-V cache, sorry.

[02:30] Raj: Important for us: we run in a hybrid model, some sensitive flows must stay in a private VPC — others can be hosted. How seamless is the same API across both?

[02:45] Jordan: Same API. You pin model versions and runtime config per environment. The Console shows per-route policies — you can say route /invoices uses private deployment with stricter encryption, while /summaries uses hosted. We'll demo that.

[03:14] Jordan: Jumping into the Console — I'm going to open the typed-response workspace. Note: demo traffic is synthetic.
[03:30] [screen share noise] Jordan: Here we have an example schema — a payment reconciliation object. Fields: invoice_id (string), total_cents (integer), currency (enum), line_items (array of objects), and a field "confidence_score" typed as number between 0-1.
[03:55] Jordan: We'll show three guardrail modes: strict (reject non-conformant outputs), best-effort (attempt repair via a repair tool), and fallback (route request to a smaller deterministic model or template-based fallback).

[04:20] Lina: For our eventing system, any rejected payloads would break pipelines. So auto-repair is key for us — can we see an example?

[04:33] Jordan: Sure. I have a sample prompt that intentionally elicits a malformed response — missing total_cents and embedding a free-text amount.
[04:46] Jordan: Running... [typing]...
[05:02] [timestamped model stream noise] Jordan: The runtime detected mismatch. In strict mode it returns a 422 with a schema diff. In best-effort it invoked a repair tool (we've registered a small parser service) which parsed the free-text amount and populated total_cents. You can see the repair temperature and confidence metric in the trace.

[05:40] Raj: That repair tool — where does it run? On-hosted Redwood infra or can it be in our VPC?

[05:49] Jordan: Both. Tools can be registered as Redwood-hosted lambdas or as webhooks inside your VPC. For PII-sensitive transforms we recommend VPC-hosted tools so data never leaves your network.

[06:12] Maya: What about audit logs and KMS? We need key-level encryption and HSM-backed keys for some customers.

[06:20] Ari: Redwood Private supports customer-managed KMS and HSM integrations. Logs can be shipped to your SIEM, and we maintain tamper-evident audit trails. We also have SOC 2 Type II and ISO talk packs — I'll send the security bundle.

[06:45] Lina: Do you keep verbatim prompts in logs? That's a big red flag for us.

[06:50] Ari: By default we capture request hashes and token-level cost metrics but you can opt out of retaining full prompts; in Private deployments the decision is yours. We'll include a data retention config in the pilot SOW.

[07:10] Jordan: Back to runtime patterns — now I'll show function/tool calling with fallback orchestration. We're going to demonstrate a two-tier fallback: first fallback uses quantized cheap model (low latency but deterministic), second fallback is template-based fill using a strict parser.

[07:34] Jordan: Triggering the route now. Watch the trace pane: request enters, routed to model A (gpt-neo-x-like), long tail latency occurs, routing policy times out at 800ms, request automatically retries on model B in the dedicated pool, if that fails we fall back to template.

[07:55] Ethan: How configurable are timeouts and what about cost visibility? Our finance team wants cost per 1k predictions by route.

[08:05] Jordan: Timeouts, retry counts, and cost buckets are configurable per-route. Console has token-level cost breakdown and per-route historical perf. Redwood Optimize also suggests batching or quantization to hit a target cost per prediction.

[08:28] Lina: Can Optimize suggest a quantization profile that preserves our accuracy for classification tasks?

[08:33] Jordan: Yes — we analyze sample prompts and provide model+quantization recommendations with estimated quality delta. We also run evals against your prompt set if you provide it.

[08:55] Maya: Security question — what about SSO and SAML for RBAC? We need role separation and auditability.

[09:02] Ari: SAML/SSO integrations supported, plus fine-grained RBAC in Console. We can map groups to resource-level permissions and export audit logs for SSO sessions.

[09:28] Jordan: I'm going to show an end-to-end example where the model calls a verification tool in Auriga's VPC. The structured output includes a field, "payment_verified": boolean, and the verifier returns a signature.
[09:45] [short pause, typing]
[10:01] Jordan: The tool produced a signature. You can see the tool call trace: request payload, response, and a signed assertion. If the verifier fails, the runtime retries with exponential backoff or triggers a human review workflow — that's configurable.

[10:30] Raj: How do you protect against model hallucination in fields like invoice_id? If model invents IDs, we need deterministic cross-checking.

[10:38] Jordan: Two approaches: validation + repair tool that cross-checks against your DB, or shadow mode where Redwood calls your lookup service asynchronously to verify and then flags mismatches. For critical fields we recommend sync verification in VPC.

[11:05] Lina: What about live canaries and rollouts? We need to test schema regressions before prod.

[11:12] Jordan: Console supports canary rollouts by percentage and by sample set. You can run evals and watch quality metrics tied to your prompt dataset. If quality drops beyond thresholds, an automatic rollback occurs to the previous model.

[11:38] Maya: Any examples of customers running a mixed private/hosted model?

[11:43] Ari: Yes — one fintech customer runs sensitive auth flows in Private with KMS and uses Hosted for non-sensitive summarization. They use Redwood Optimize for batching to reduce costs.

[12:00] Ethan: Let's talk latency targets — we need 95th percentile below 300ms for the summary endpoint, but tolerate 800-1k for backoffice reconciliations. Can you meet those?

[12:12] Jordan: Depends on model and payload size. With continuous batching and KV cache warmed, for short context we can get sub-200ms on high-tier dedicated pools. For hosted, plan for slightly higher variability; you can set SLOs per-deployment. We'll work with your loadprofile to pick instance types.

[12:45] Raj: If we start a pilot, what data we'll need to share for Optimize's recommendations?

[12:51] Jordan: Sample prompts (redacted OK), traffic shape (requests per minute, 95th percentile), and a small labeled eval set if possible. We analyze token distributions and recommend batching/quant settings.

[13:12] Jordan: I'm going to flip to the API quickstart — the same route we saw in Console can be invoked with a one-liner cURL.
[13:22] Jordan: Example payload: {"prompt":"...","schema":"/schemas/payment-v1.json","guardrail_mode":"best-effort","tools":["verifier-svc"]}. Notice schema reference is URI; the runtime resolves and validates.

[13:48] Lina: We have strict compliance windows — procurement needs pricing anchors and SLA clauses.

[13:54] Ari: We'll draft pilot SOW with pricing tiers: hosted pay-as-you-go, reserved Dedicated commits, and Private licensing. SLA options vary by deployment; Dedicated gets latency/uptime SLAs. I'll include a pricing spreadsheet.

[14:15] Maya: Also need data processing agreement and subprocessor list.

[14:20] Ari: Yep — will include DPA and subprocessors.

[14:30] Jordan: Quick note on developer ergonomics — we provide SDKs that emit typed client bindings from your JSON schema so engineers get native objects and compile-time checks. That reduces runtime surprises.

[14:52] Ethan: Will that bind to our language stack? We're mostly Python + Go.

[14:56] Jordan: We generate bindings for Python, TS/Node, and Go.

[15:10] Lina: One more question about fallback metrics — if a request falls back to a template, can we see that proportion in dashboards? We need to alert if fallbacks exceed 2%.

[15:20] Jordan: Yes, fallback rates are first-class metrics and you can set alerts. We also surface the reason code (timeout, schema-mismatch, model-error).

[15:38] [brief side discussion about shared docs and links]
[15:50] Ari: I'll share the pilot SOW, security pack, and a sample schema repo. Jordan will drop the example schema and repair tool code snippet. We'll also propose benchmark windows.

[16:05] Lina: Timeline-wise, we'd like a 4-week pilot starting mid-September with a two week evaluation and a final readout. Procurement wants to budget in Q4.

[16:15] Ari: Sounds doable. Pilot would be scoped: environment setup (VPC or hosted decision), sample prompts ingest, Optimize analysis, runtime guardrail config, and a 2-week benchmark run.

[16:32] Raj: For the benchmark run we'll need instance sizing and a plan to replay traffic — can Redwood replay using recorded traces?

[16:38] Jordan: Yes, we can replay traces into a sandboxed deployment and measure p95, p99, and token-level cost. We'll coordinate with your infra team for credentials.

[16:55] Maya: Security will want to validate the replay process — ensure no sensitive tokens are re-injected.

[17:02] Jordan: Replay can scrub secrets; we support redaction rules.

[17:12] Ari: To recap — action items and next steps: Ari to send SOW/pricing/security pack; Jordan to share schema examples, repair tool sample, and runtime config snippets; Auriga to confirm pilot start week and provide traffic samples and eval set.

[17:28] Lina: Agreed. Also we want an initial list of stakeholders for procurement and legal loops.

[17:35] Ari: Please send me the stakeholders and I'll cc them on the SOW.

[17:42] Ethan: Quick note — are there any known limitations with very deep nested arrays in schemas? We've seen some LLMs struggle.

[17:49] Jordan: Deeply nested structures increase generation variance; recommended patterns: normalize into flatter objects, or require a two-step flow where model emits pointers and a deterministic tool materializes nested expansions. We'll document patterns.

[18:10] Raj: One last operational Q: how does KV cache warming work if we scale from 0 to peak? We have bursty traffic.

[18:18] Jordan: Cache warming can be primed via offline batches or on-demand warmers. For bursty patterns we recommend a small warm pool and pre-warm with representative keys. KV cache evictions are LRU and metrics show hit rate; Optimize suggests optimal pool sizes.

[18:40] Lina: Cool. If there are no other questions we can wrap.

[18:47] Maya: All good from security side for now.
[18:50] Raj: Nothing else.

[18:55] Ari: Thanks everyone — we'll follow up with materials.

[19:02] Jordan: I'll post the schema repo link in the meeting notes, expect example repair tool and fallback configs.

[19:10] Lina: Thanks, talk soon.

[19:15] (meeting ends)
